He said, "I am happy." (Indirect)
o: He said that I was happy.
He said that he was happy.

mcq.q: They said, "They will come tomorrow." (Indirect)
o: They said that they would come the next day.
They said that they will come tomorrow.
They said they would come tomorrow.
They told that they will come the next day.

mcq.q: Our teacher said, "The sun rises in the east." (Indirect)
o: Our teacher said that the sun rose in the east.
Our teacher said that the sun rises in the east.
Our teacher said that the sun had risen in the east.
Our teacher told the sun rises in the east.

mcq.q: He said, "Where are you going?" (Indirect)
o: He asked where I was going.
He asked where was I going.
He said where I am going.
He asked where I am going.

mcq.q: My friend said to me, "Let us watch a documentary." (Indirect)
o: My friend proposed to me that we should watch a documentary.
My friend said let us watch a documentary.
My friend ordered me to watch a documentary.
My friend asked that we watch a documentary.

Explain the stanzas of ‘If’ with reference to the context. The Dear Departed (Play): Long Questions
What do the actions and words of Mrs. Slater and Mrs. Jordan reveal about their true motivations? How do these motivations influence their behaviour throughout the play?
How does the conflict over Mr. Merryweather's possessions drive the plot of the play? What does this conflict reveal about the characters' values and priorities?
In what ways does Stanley Houghton use satire to criticize family dynamics and social values in the play? How effective is this approach in conveying his message?
How does the play challenge the traditional idea of family unity and affection? What does The Dear Departed suggest about the nature of family ties when material wealth is involved?
What role does the clock on the mantelpiece play in the story? How might it symbolize the characters' attitude towards time, routine, or even inheritance?
How does Victoria's character differ from the adults' around her? What does her perspective tell us about the younger generation's view of the family's behaviour?
How do the characters display hypocrisy throughout the play? What are some examples where their words contradict their actions?

How does the setting of the play — a single, confined living room — affect the way the characters interact with each other? What might this confined space suggest about the nature of their relationships?
How does Stanley Houghton organise the sequence of events in The Dear Departed to build tension and reveal the characters' true motives?
How do the themes of The Dear Departed remain relevant in modern society? Can you think of contemporary examples where materialism impacts family relationships in a similar way? Lesson
What does the title ‘The Dear Departed’ suggest about the play's theme, and how is it ironic in the context of the story?
What role does humour play in ‘The Dear Departed’? How does Houghton use humour to convey serious themes like family conflict and hypocrisy? Letters
